events.description:
Organized and hosted by the Center for Medieval and Early Modern Studies (CMEMS).

Reviel Netz (Classics, Stanford) presents, "The Shaping of Modern Science: Paper Practices in the 17th Century"

Event Sponsor: Program in History and Philosophy of Science

With a response from Yoav Levinson-Sela (History, Stanford). See the abstract below.

Koyré, discovering that Galileo and Descartes both moved in parallel towards the discovery of the law of free fall – but that only Galileo made it – used this to identify Galileo’s originality as the first to form the specifically dynamic concepts of modern physics. The more recent realization - that Thomas Harriot, too, made the same discovery as Galileo, following a similar path, and a similarly protracted campaign – should help us see the historical originality not in terms of shared concepts, but instead of shared practices. Everyone involved – Descartes, Galileo, Harriot – pursued protracted campaigns based on curating paper archives for which there were no ancient or medieval antecedents. The thesis proposed by the talk, then, is bold: that modern science was shaped by its new paper practices.

events.title: Video Game Character Creation, or Do I Have To Be a White Guy?
events.description:
The video game character creation screen represents the clearest aesthetic iteration of the medium’s promise of agency. The player is given the ability to create a self-insert character or a fantastical projection and then become whoever they want to be within the game world curated by the designer. Yet, the UI design of character creation screens undercuts that promise of agency by typically making the default created character align with the typical video game protagonist: white, male, muscular, and conventionally attractive. Combining both qualitative readings of select character creation screens with quantitative analysis of a larger corpus of character creators, this talk explores the default created character presented in over 200 video games from 1984 to 2026, spanning genres from the CRPG to the cozy sim to the sports game. In doing so, the talk asks if the standard default starting character creates and sustains a racial aesthetic, one in which the player is always implicitly a white guy.

About the Speaker

Austin Anderson PhD is a Provostial Fellow at Stanford University and Director of the Stanford Critical Game Studies Lab. He studies how games are enmeshed with race, gender, and class while also examining the liberatory potentials of gameworlds. His first book project, Racial Recursivity: A Methodology for Critical Race Game Studies, creates a formalist framework for analyzing the racial aesthetics of videogames. He has published in the fields of game studies, African American literary studies, and comic studies, and his work has appeared in the Journal of Gaming & Virtual Worlds, Transformative Works and Culture, Electronic Book Review, KULA, The Comparatist, Popular Culture Review, ADE Bulletin, ASAP/Review, and other outlets. He currently serves on the Multiplay Editorial Board and the SCMS Precarious Labor Committee.

events.description:
What is the relationship between capitalism and freedom in the United States? This question has motivated a generation of scholars who have looked to the history of American slavery to better understand the origins of American capitalism. But scholars have yet to fully grapple with the ways in which enslaved people, both as property and as economic agents, understood the complicated logics of American capitalism. This presentation, organized in collaboration with the Slavery and Freedom workshop, considers the centrality of enslaved people's lived experiences to the history of capitalism in the United States.

Professor Justene Hill Edwards is Professor of History at the University of Virginia. She is the author of Savings and Trust: The Rise and Betrayal of the Freedman's Bank (Norton, 2024) and Unfree Markets: The Slaves' Economy and the Rise of Capitalism in South Carolina (Columbia University Press, 2021). She received her PhD from Princeton University.

The lecture will be followed by comments from Stanford Professor Kathryn Olivarius, a historian of the nineteenth-century United States whose research examines the intersections of slavery, capitalism, and medicine.

events.title: Wild & Bright: Designing for Belonging | Artist Talk with Yiying Lu, in Conversation with Thomas S. Mullaney
events.description:
What can a whale, a dumpling, and an endangered clouded leopard tell us about belonging?

Join artist and designer Yiying Lu, creator of Twitter’s Fail Whale and six emoji adopted into the Unicode Standard, for an opening talk celebrating Wild & Bright, an exhibition of nine large-scale digital paintings from her multi-year series on endangered species, on view in Hohbach Hall at Green Library through 2028.

Lu will trace the unexpected creative path connecting these seemingly different worlds: from a personal illustration that became Twitter’s Fail Whale in 2008, to emoji designed to expand the world’s shared visual vocabulary, to a red panda created for a Bay Area AAPI night market that opened an entirely new direction in her practice.

That exploration eventually led Lu to the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity, where her logo design for COP15 received an Award of Honor, and to support from the Adobe Creative Residency Community Fund. Wild & Bright began on August 4, 2020, International Clouded Leopard Day, with the clouded leopard as the first animal in the series.

The work has since returned to the community in new ways. In 2025, sixteen pieces from the series were featured at a San Francisco Zoo fundraising gala, bringing art, storytelling, and wildlife conservation together.

Across Lu’s work runs a central question:

What does it take to make someone, or something, feel like it belongs in the picture?

She approaches belonging as a design inquiry: whether the subject is a species losing its natural habitat, a culture missing from a global visual language, or a whale that made failure feel unexpectedly human.

Following the presentation, Lu will join Professor Thomas S. Mullaney for a conversation about language, technology, and how visual systems decide who becomes visible. The program will conclude with an audience Q&A.

The event takes place in the lead-up to World Animal Day on October 4.

About Yiying Lu

Yiying Lu is an award-winning artist, designer, and creative leader working at the intersection of art, technology, culture, and human experience. For nearly two decades, her practice has moved across digital culture, brand systems, public art, creative technology, and civic life, translating complex ideas into visual experiences that connect across cultures and communities.

She is the creator of Twitter’s Fail Whale and has designed and successfully proposed six emoji adopted into the Unicode Standard, including the dumpling and boba tea. She previously served as Global Creative Director at 500 Global and as a San Francisco Arts Commissioner, appointed by the Mayor of San Francisco. She currently leads Happy Creative Land, a San Francisco-based innovation studio, and serves as an Adobe Global Creative Ambassador and a committee member of the UNESCO Chair in Digital Futures at Stanford.

Her creative collaborations have included Disney, Apple, Google, Airbnb, Adobe, and NYU Shanghai. She has spoken at SXSW, Web Summit, TEDx, Today at Apple, and Talks at Google, and her work has been featured in The New York Times, BBC, TIME, The Atlantic, WIRED, and The Wall Street Journal.

Lu has been recognized by Fast Company as one of its Most Creative People in Business, by Microsoft as a Top 10 Leader in Innovation, and by the Shorty Awards as its inaugural winner in Design.

Born in Shanghai, educated in Sydney and London, and based in San Francisco, Lu brings a lived global perspective to the ways design and storytelling can create connections across cultures, communities, and generations.

About Thomas Mullaney

Thomas S. Mullaney is Professor of History and Professor of East Asian Languages and Cultures, by courtesy. He is also the Kluge Chair in Technology and Society at the Library of Congress, and a Guggenheim Fellow.

He is the author or lead editor of 7 books, including The Chinese Typewriter (winner of the Fairbank prize), Your Computer is on Fire, Coming to Terms with the Nation: Ethnic Classification in Modern China, and the forthcoming The Chinese Computer—the first comprehensive history of Chinese-language computing.

His writings have appeared in the Journal of Asian Studies, Technology & Culture, Aeon, Foreign Affairs, and Foreign Policy, and his work has been featured in the LA Times, The Atlantic, the BBC, and in invited lectures at Google, Microsoft, Adobe, and more. He holds a PhD from Columbia University.

events.title: Andrew Shen | Unlocking LLM Creativity in Science through Analogical Reasoning
events.description:
Abstract

Autonomous science promises to augment scientific discovery, particularly in complex fields like biomedicine. However, this requires AI systems that can consistently generate novel and diverse solutions to open-ended problems. We evaluate LLMs on the task of open-ended solution generation and quantify their tendency to mode collapse into low-diversity generations. To mitigate this mode collapse, we introduce analogical reasoning (AR) as a new approach to solution generation. AR generates analogies to cross-domain problems based on shared relational structure, then uses those analogies to search for novel solutions. Compared to baselines, AR discovers significantly more diverse generations (improving solution diversity metrics by 90-173%), generates novel solutions over 50% of the time (compared to as little as 1.6% for baselines), and produces high-quality analogies. To validate the real-world feasibility of AR, we implement AR-generated solutions across four biomedical problems, yielding consistent quantitative gains. AR-generated approaches achieve a nearly 13-fold improvement on distributional metrics for perturbation effect prediction, outperform all baselines on AUPRC when predicting cell-cell communication, infer brain region interactions with a high Spearman correlation (ρ=0.729) to published methods, and establish state-of-the-art performance on 2 datasets for oligonucleotide property prediction. The novel and diverse solutions produced by AR can be used to augment the search space of existing solution generation methods.

Bio

Andrew is a second-year PhD student in Biomedical Data Science at Stanford, advised by James Zou. He is broadly interested in problems at the intersection of AI and science, and his current work focuses on autonomous scientific discovery. Before Stanford, he was a research associate with Marinka Zitnik at Harvard Medical School, where he developed machine learning methods for medicine and science, including work on evolutionary reasoning of protein language models and molecular AI generalizability. He completed a MS in Artificial Intelligence from Northwestern University and a BS in Bioinformatics from UC San Diego.

The Center for Neural Data Science Seminar Series is a platform for trainees across campus to share insights and innovative approaches that bridge the gap between neuroscience and data science.

events.title: Sustainable Systems Seminar Lunch Series - ElectriPedia: Mapping Electrification Progress at Scale via LLM-Enabled Building Permit Mining
events.description:
This week's speaker is:

Sam Bobick, Ph.D. Student, Stanford University

"ElectriPedia: Mapping Electrification Progress at Scale via LLM-Enabled Building Permit Mining"

Abstract:

Electrification shifts heating, cooking, and transportation from fossil fuels to electricity, yielding emissions reductions as the grid decarbonizes and consumers adopt distributed energy resources such as rooftop solar and batteries. In this talk, I will introduce ElectriPedia, a nationwide, address-level electrification dataset derived from unstructured building permit descriptions. Applied nationwide, ElectriPedia identifies 33.3 million technology instances across 12.8 million addresses. By providing spatially and temporally detailed visibility into electrification adoption, ElectriPedia can enable applications that are difficult or impossible with less granular datasets, including more targeted infrastructure planning, improved grid operations, equitable policy design, and tracking of electrification progress.

Bio:

Sam Bobick is a PhD student in Civil and Environmental Engineering advised by Ram Rajagopal. His work applies data-driven methods including machine learning, econometrics, optimization, and control to challenges in energy systems. He received a B.A. in Computer Science from UC Berkeley in 2025 and is an NSF Graduate Research Fellow.

The topics of this seminar are broad but typically fall under technologies’ scaling potential and impact on (the system of) people, the environment and the economy. A particular focus is placed on the interaction potential of technologies with the energy, water, and material systems. Our goal is to create an intimate, collaborative space for students, postdocs, scientists, and PIs within Stanford across micro-level (material and technology) to macro-level (system) interests. These seminars will provide an opportunity to disseminate insights from your studies, connect with fellow researchers, and strengthen bonds across the community.

events.title: Distinguished Lecture Series Lunch Talk | Two Modes of Sedentism on the Tibetan Plateau
events.description:
Each quarter, the Stanford Archaeology Center invites prominent archaeologists from around the globe to be in residence for a week as a Distinguished Lecturer. During their residency, the Distinguished Lecturer gives two lectures and interacts with faculty, postdoctoral scholars and students. Stanford Archaeology Center will host Prof. Xiaoyan Yang Lanzhou University over two days (Oct 7 and Oct 8 for the Fall Quarter of this academic year.

Abstract:

Sedentism is one of the milestone events in the development of human society. Settlement in ultra-high-altitude regions reflects human physiological and cultural adaptation to extreme environments. Through morphological identification, isotopic analysis, and ancient DNA analysis of faunal and floral remains from the Lapo site (2800 m a.s.l., 4800 BP) and the Mabu Co site (4420–4460 m a.s.l., 4400 BP) on the Tibetan Plateau, we discovered that the process of sedentism on the plateau followed at least two distinct modes. In relatively low-altitude river valleys, intensive millet pig agriculture supported early settlement, whereas in high-altitude regions where crop cultivation is not possible, a fishing hunting economy centered on lake resources initiated the sedentism process.

events.description:

A cell-type-specific cortical circuit for maintenance of value representations
Abstract
Our decisions are shaped by the history of our choices and their outcomes. To guide future behavior, the brain must maintain information about past experience, update it as new outcomes are encountered, and use it when selecting subsequent actions. How neural circuits accomplish these computations remains poorly understood.
We study the neural mechanisms underlying history-dependent decision-making in mice performing value-based behavior. Using longitudinal imaging and circuit manipulations, our work has identified the retrosplenial cortex as an important site for maintaining information about the value of behavioral options across trials. More recent experiments investigate how distinct neuronal populations and local and long-range circuit interactions contribute to the maintenance and use of this information.
I will discuss these findings and their implications for how cortical circuits maintain internal variables over time and transform past experience into future actions.

Takaki Komiyama
Professor of Neurobiology and Neurosciences, University of California, San Diego
Takaki Komiyama is a Professor of Neurobiology and Neurosciences at the University of California, San Diego. His research seeks to understand how neural circuits enable learning and adaptive behavior, with a particular focus on how experience modifies cortical circuits. His laboratory combines advanced optical imaging, electrophysiology, circuit manipulation, behavioral approaches, and computational analysis to study the neural mechanisms underlying motor learning, decision-making, and perceptual learning.
Dr. Komiyama received his B.A. from the University of Tokyo and Ph.D. from Stanford University, where he studied neural circuit development. He subsequently conducted postdoctoral research at the Janelia Research Campus, developing approaches to examine the activity and plasticity of cortical circuits during learning. He joined the faculty at UC San Diego in 2010.
His work has revealed principles by which neural activity and synaptic connectivity are reorganized through learning and how these processes are altered by aging and neurological disease.

events.description:
The core neural circuit for learning to predict
Abstract
The ability to predict future outcomes is a fundamental basis of flexible behavior. In the brain, the neuromodulator dopamine is thought to play a central role in learning to predict future rewards. A large body of evidence suggests that dopamine supports this predictive learning by signaling a moment-by-moment prediction error, called a temporal difference (TD) error, analogous to those used in reinforcement learning algorithms. However, whether reinforcement learning algorithms are truly implemented in the brain, and if so how, remains unclear. In this talk, I will present our recent work addressing two key issues: (1) how dopamine signals are computed, and (2) how core parameters of reinforcement learning models may be instantiated within neural circuits.
Naoshige Uchida
Jeff C. Tarr Professor of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Harvard University (website)
Naoshige Uchida is a Jeff C. Tarr Professor and Chair of Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology at Harvard University. He received his Ph.D. from Kyoto University in Japan, where he worked on the molecular mechanism of synaptic adhesions in Masatoshi Takeichi’s laboratory. He studied olfactory coding in Kensaku Mori’s laboratory at the RIKEN Center for Brain Science in Japan. He then joined Zachary F. Mainen’s laboratory at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, where he developed psychophysical olfactory decision tasks in rodents. He started his laboratory at Harvard University in 2006. Uchida’s current research focuses on the neurobiology of decision-making and learning. In particular, his laboratory has studied the midbrain dopamine system using computational modeling with reinforcement learning theories.

About the Seminar:

Policy on young people and technology has been gaining momentum, on the assumption that what adolescents do online is the problem to be removed. This talk starts from the opposite premise: young people turn to technology to meet the developmental needs that define adolescence, their identity, relationships, and mental health. Drawing on existing and ongoing empirical work, Anthony Chen argues that technology use is better read as information about what young people need than as the reason they are struggling. These findings may change what schools, families, and regulators think they should do as young people navigate the technology world.

Anthony Chen is a postdoctoral scholar at the Tech Impact and Policy Center. His research examines how social media and emerging technologies shape identity, relationships, and well-being, with a particular focus on adolescents and young adults. The Global Studies in Migration & Diaspora Research Workshop is excited to announce that our first event this autumn will feature Moustafa Bayoumi, Professor of English at Brooklyn College (CUNY), Stanford Humanities Center External Faculty Fellow, and author of How Does It Feel To Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. Join us to learn more about Professor Bayoumi's work, "'I can’t imagine living next to a wall': Palestine and the Tohono O’odham Nation." This piece informs his forthcoming book project, Like a Palestinian: How the Idea of Palestine Has Changed in—and Is Changing—America. Dinner will be served for those who RSVP.

Abstract: The Tohono O’odham Nation is a 2.8-million-acre reservation in the Sonoran Desert in southern Arizona established in 1916 for the Tohono O’odham people. With its 62-mile boundary with Mexico, the Nation has the longest international border of any Indigenous group along the US-Mexico frontier. For many years, O’odham activists have noticed that the fight for O’odham rights and lands parallels the struggle for Palestinian rights and land. Both the Tohono O’odham people and the Palestinians people are haunted by a recurring politics of premature death. Both live under pervasive regimes of surveillance and survive under states of siege. Both have seen their lands taken from them and justified by military necessity. And both have also had to face their worlds being hemmed in by massive, isolating border walls. This lecture explores these parallels and investigates the current fight the O’odham people are waging to secure their rights and oppose construction of the US government’s border wall on their land.

events.title: Art History Lightning Talks
events.description:
Presented by the Department of Art & Art History, this art history lightning talk event features three distinguished alums—Altair Brandon-Salmon, Alisa Eagleston-Cieslewicz, and Sabrina Buell. Each alum will give a 15-minute presentation on their work and area of expertise, followed by a brief 5-minute discussion. From curatorial research and art conservation to art advising and public collections, the talks highlight the diverse career paths and perspectives of Stanford Art History graduates. The event will be moderated by Head Librarian Lindsay King.

EVENT PROGRAM

Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail

Speaker: Altair Brandon-Salmon (PhD ’24)

In 1938, the National Gallery in London published One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery, written by its young director, Kenneth Clark (1903-83). Old Master paintings in the collection were presented as cropped, black-and-white pairs. The book, with its witty commentary and beautiful production, was a huge success.

This curator’s talk will illuminate the Bowes Art and Architecture Library’s exhibition Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail, which is the first to take One Hundred Details as the lynchpin to understand how details—cropped reproductions of paintings—were central to looking at art in the early 20th century. From the groundbreaking work of art historians to avant-garde publications, the exhibition shows that these monochrome details, published facing one another across a page spread, created a distinctive, modernist way of seeing Old Master painting.

Altair Brandon-Salmon is an art historian and a lecturer in Civic, Liberal, and Global Education at Stanford University. His scholarship on modern art has appeared in Art History, Art Journal, British Art Studies, and the Oxford Art Journal. He has been a curator for the Sheldonian Theatre and Campion Hall, University of Oxford, and he is currently a guest curator for Projects Twenty Two. His book, Rubble: Art, the Blitz, and London in Ruins, is forthcoming in spring 2027.

Setting Art Up For Success: A Career in Art Conservation

Speaker: Alisa Eagleston-Cieslewicz (BA ‘04)

Art Conservators often think about how their actions will impact artworks many years from now. Throughout her career in art conservation and museum administration, Alisa Eagleston-Cieslewicz (‘04) has brought this long-term perspective to the conservation of individual artworks, public art installations, and museum administration. This talk will look at how considering the long-term interaction of art-making materials, conservation choices, and exhibition sites can strengthen the preservation and maintenance of artworks, particularly in public installations and private collections.

Alisa Eagleston-Cieslewicz holds a MA in art history with an advanced certificate in art conservation from the Institute of Fine Arts, New York University and an MBA from the Haas School of Business at UC Berkeley. She has held positions at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, SFO Museum, and The Foster Museum. She is currently an objects conservator and museum consultant in private practice at Mayfield Art Conservation and Consulting LLC, where she works with museums and collectors to conserve their artworks and to build the institutional infrastructure to support ongoing collections care. Alisa also serves on the Historic Resources Board for the City of Palo Alto and on the board of the Bay Area Art Conservation Guild.

Building a Collection: the Eye, the Market, and Public Art at Stanford

Speaker: Sabrina Buell (BA ’99)

Sabrina Buell will trace her path at the intersection of art and business, from studying Art History and Economics at Stanford through her 25 years in the business as an Advisor to many of the most important public and private collections of our time. Chief among the public collections she and her firm have advised is Stanford University. She will speak about the growing public art collection on campus, the Denning House collection for the Knight-Hennessy scholars, and Stanford’s commitment to the arts on campus going forward.

Sabrina Buell founded Zlot Buell + Associates, a cross-generational, multifaceted art advisory firm, in 2012. She was previously a Director at Matthew Marks Gallery in New York for 10 years. Sabrina grew up in San Francisco and holds degrees from Stanford University and NYU.

events.title: Nicholas Branigan | Non-ergodicity and Simpson’s paradox in neural correlates
events.description:
Abstract

What are the neural correlates of human behavior? Much research has approached versions of this question between individuals but not within individuals (over time). Are results from these 2 approaches similar? To address this, we mapped the neural correlates of 4 cognitive measures both between and within individuals in over 4000 people. We combined fMRI with a probabilistic model of the stop signal task that we developed to capture trial-level variation in cognitive measures. For each of these measures, neural correlates diverged between versus within individuals—a striking example of non-ergodicity and Simpson’s paradox. For example, individuals with worse control had less brain activity, but when an individual had worse control they had more brain activity. I’ll argue that non-ergodicity creates both challenges and opportunities for human neuroscience. Studies relying on individual-average measures have left unanswered fundamental questions about temporal dynamics. This means that our picture of the neural correlates of cognition and disease may be dramatically incomplete, but it also suggests that new discoveries could come from experiments and models that now target within-individual variation.

Bio

Nicholas is a Research Data Analyst at Stanford with Vinod Menon. He is interested in developing methods to understand large-scale behavioral and brain data. He has worked on developing probabilistic machine learning models, including drift-diffusion models of cognitive control and state-space models of fMRI and calcium imaging. Before falling for neuroscience, Nicholas worked in experimental economics with Muriel Niederle and philanthropic strategy with Paul Brest. He received an MS in statistics and a BA in economics, both from Stanford.

events.title: David Anderson - Neural Coding of Affective Internal States Underlying Innate Behaviors
events.description:
Join the speaker for coffee, cookies, and conversation before the talk, starting at 11:45am.
Neural Coding of Affective Internal States Underlying Innate Behaviors
Abstract
Innate survival behaviors such as fighting, mating and predator defense are associated with affective or emotion states. Finding neural representations of such states using supervised analyses is challenging due to a lack of direct state measures. To overcome this limitations, we have performed unsupervised modeling of single-trial neural data acquired during naturalistic social behaviors, using recurrent Switching Linear Dynamical Systems (rSLDS). rSLDS learns a dynamics matrix based on latent factor activity in a state-space approximated by a set of linear substates, yielding a probabilistic model of neural dynamics. When used to model single-trial calcium imaging data recorded from hypothalamic “attack” neurons during aggressive encounters, rSLDS discovered an approximate line attractor that represents the intensity and duration of a scalable and persistent state of aggressiveness. I will discuss features of this representation, evidence for its local instantiation in the hypothalamus, mechanistic implementation and generalization to other social behaviors. Together, these results extend the potential role of line attractor dynamics beyond the representation of cognitive variables, to the representation of affective internal states. They also identify a tractable experimental platform to investigate how circuit-level mechanisms give rise to emergent network dynamics at the manifold level in the mammalian brain.

David Anderson
Professor of Biology, TianQiao and Chrissy Chen Leadership Chair, HHMI Investigator, California Institute of Technology
David J. Anderson received his AB in Biochemical Sciences, Summa Cum Laude, from Harvard College in 1978. He received his Ph.D. in Cell Biology with Dr. Günter Blobel at The Rockefeller University in 1982 and did postdoctoral work with Dr. Richard Axel at Columbia University from 1983-1986. He joined the faculty of Caltech as an Assistant Professor of Biology in 1986 and has remained there ever since. In 1989 he was appointed an Assistant Investigator of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. In 1992 he was promoted to Associate Professor (with tenure) at Caltech and Associate Investigator at HHMI and in 1996 promoted to Full Professor and HHMI Investigator. He is currently the Seymour Benzer Professor of Biology and has been the Tianqiao and Chrissy Chen Leadership Chair and Director of the Tianqiao and Chrissy Chen Institute for Neuroscience at Caltech since 2017. He has received the 1999 Alden Spencer Award in Neurobiology from Columbia University, the 2017 Perl-UNC Neuroscience Prize, the 2017 Thomas Salmon Award from the New York Academy of Medicine and the 2018 Edward M. Scolnick Prize in Neuroscience from MIT. In 2002 he was elected a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and of the American Association for the Advancement of Science. In 2007 he was elected as a member of the US National Academy of Sciences. Dr. Anderson was a founding scientific advisor of the Allen Institute for Brain Science and proposed the Institute’s inaugural project, a complete map of gene expression in the murine brain. Dr. Anderson has authored over 250 research articles and has published two books: The Neuroscience of Emotion: A New Synthesis (co-authored with Ralph Adolphs) (2018, Princeton University Press) and The Nature of the Beast: How Emotions Guide Us (2022, Basic Books). He resides in Altadena, California.

events.title: Emily Jacobs - New frontiers in women's brain health
events.description:
Join the speaker for coffee, cookies, and conversation before the talk, starting at 11:45am.
New frontiers in women's brain health
Abstract
Gonadal hormones are potent neuromodulators of learning and memory. Yet, how these tiny molecules shape the structural and functional architecture of the human brain is virtually unknown. Many brain imaging studies miss a central feature of the endocrine system: hormone production ebbs and flows over time. Precision imaging allows us to map the mammalian brain with exquisite temporal resolution. Following individuals across major endocrine transitions, like the circadian cycle, menstrual cycle, and pregnancy, these studies reveal the human brain's capacity for rapid reorganization and hormones' role in shaping this process.
Jacobs' talk also considers why women’s health research is decades behind where it should be. Nowhere is this knowledge gap more visible than in neuroscience, where fewer than 0.5% of brain imaging articles focus on female-specific experiences, including menstruation, pregnancy, and menopause, that shape the lives of half the global population (Jacobs Nature 2023). Progress in women’s health will require a global shift in science culture, and that shift has started. Jacobs will examine emerging research programs, public policy changes, and private sector funding opportunities that are shining a floodlight on women’s health, and by doing so are opening up new frontiers for understanding health and disease.

Emily Jacobs, PhD
Professor Jacobs, University of California, Santa Barbara
Emily Jacobs is a Professor of Neuroscience at UC Santa Barbara and Director of the Ann S. Bowers Women's Brain Health Initiative. Her body of research examines dynamic endocrine modulation of the nervous system. In 2024 her team published the first detailed view of the human brain across pregnancy and she leads several multi-center studies on neurological changes tied to menopause. Prior to UCSB, she held a faculty appointment at Harvard Medical School and the Department of Medicine/Division of Women's Health at Brigham & Women's Hospital. She serves on the Steering Committee of the Coalition for Women’s Brain Health, the Milken Institute’s Women’s Health Network, the Foundation for Women’s Health, and the WHAM Research Collaborative to drive the national and international agenda on women’s health research. In recognition of her work, she was named a Robert Wood Johnson Foundation Health and Society Scholar, a National Institutes of Health Women's Health Fellow, a National Academy of Sciences Frontiers of Science Kavli Fellow and Science News’ “Top 10 Scientists” to watch. Outside of the lab, Dr. Jacobs’ team partners with K-12 groups to advance girls' representation in STEM. You can find her work in the The New York Times, National Geographic, Scientific American, NPR, BBC, TED, Radiolab, Netflix, and MasterClass. She is a graduate of Smith and UC Berkeley.

events.title: Elizabeth Jun (Nuyujukian Lab) & Lavonna Mark (Giocomo Lab)
events.description:
Elizabeth Jun
PhD Student, Nuyujukian Lab, Stanford University (profile, lab website)
Elizabeth Jun is a neuroscience PhD Candidate at Stanford University and NIH F31 Predoctoral Fellow funded through National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS). Her research interests lie in understanding how large networks of neurons coordinate together to perform computations and support a wide range of behaviors in different contexts. Specifically in her thesis work, advised by Dr. Paul Nuyujukian in the Brain Interfacing Laboratory, she aims to understand how the brain can flexibly support a wide range of complex movements that are supported by a fixed set of fundamental motor computations. She is interested in connecting features of high-dimensional population data to similar behaviors in different contexts, and exploring in general how high-dimensional population features relate back to properties of the neural circuit.
Investigating preserved neural motifs across and within tasks in premotor cortex
Abstract
Motor systems neuroscience studies how populations of motor cortical neurons coordinate to perform motor computations, but less is known about how large repertoires of movements are flexibly generated from a fixed set of fundamental motor computations. There is an emerging idea of conserved neural “modules”, or recurring neural activity patterns deploying computations through dynamics, that may serve as elementary building blocks for performing the same fundamental computation across a wide array of contexts. However, exactly what feature of neural dynamics is “recurring” and fundamentally conserved, if any, when performing the same motor computation within a wide range of reach sequence and kinematic contexts has yet to be shown and characterized empirically.
To investigate this, we trained an animal implanted with a 96-channel Utah array in premotor cortex to perform 4 visually guided arm reaching motor tasks that are composed of unique combinations of 5 distinct motor processes (preparation, initiation, execution, hold, error correction) implemented in various reach conditions, where the same process can reappear across tasks and reappear again within tasks. This design allows us to test the hypothesis that premotor dynamics reuse conserved neural dynamics for performing the same motor computational process, but potentially implemented in different locations and orientations in population state space when reperformed across tasks, repeated in a sequence within tasks, and in different kinematic conditions. In this talk, I will explore systematically testing this hypothesis for all 5 motor processes to understand whether there are general organizing principles for premotor dynamics associated with deploying the same fundamental motor computation in a range of tasks, sequences, and kinematic contexts.

events.description:
The Girand Center for Biomedical Ethics is pleased to announce this year’s speaker, Dr. Bryant Lin, in conversation with Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider, for the 36th Annual Jonathan J. King Lecture.

We invite you to join us on Thursday, November 5 at 5:30pm PT in the Cedar Room at the Stanford Faculty Club or via livestream for My Cancer Journey: Happiness and Sadness, Hope and Fear.

In this talk, Dr. Lin will share a candid and deeply personal reflection on living with terminal cancer. As a leading researcher, cancer advocate, and patient, he brings a rare perspective to the realities of serious illness, clinical care, hope, and what it means to live fully in the face of uncertainty. Joining Dr. Lin is Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider, a physician, journalist, producer, and leading voice in compassionate, patient-centered care. Together, Dr. Lin and Dr. Ungerleider will explore the emotional and practical dimensions of a cancer diagnosis—including fear, purpose, relationships, and the ways we navigate life-limiting illness with honesty and humanity.

Special book launch opportunity: In-person attendees will have the opportunity to purchase signed copies of Dr. Lin’s new book, Sunshine: An Exploration of Living When You Are Dying, releasing November 10. Hors d’oeuvres and refreshments will also be served following the program.

We hope to see you there!

About the speakers

Bryant Lin, MD, MEng is a primary care physician, educator and researcher. The cornerstone of Dr. Lin's work is keeping medicine focused on humans - patients, providers, families and trainees - and not lost in technology and algorithms. His research and educational interests span (1) Developing and testing novel medical technologies, (2) Improving the health of Asian populations with Precision and Population Health, and (3) Increasing expression and interconnections in the Health Community with the Humanities and Arts. In 2018, he co-founded and currently co-directs, with Dr. Latha Palaniappan, the Center for Asian Health Research and Education (CARE) which aims to improve the health of Asians everywhere. In 2021, Dr. Lin was appointed the Director of Medical Humanities and Arts at Stanford Medicine. In 2024, he was diagnosed with Stage 4 Lung Cancer and started a medical school class based on his experience receiving national media attention including from the New York Times and CBS Morning. He is the author of the upcoming book "Sunshine: An Exploration of Living When You Are Dying".

Shoshana Ungerleider, MD, is an internal medicine physician, journalist, producer, and leading voice on end-of-life care and the future of healthcare. She is the founder and board president of the End Well Foundation, a nonprofit dedicated to making end of life a part of life, and is the host and producer of the TED Health and Before We Go podcasts. Dr. Ungerleider is a frequent medical expert on CNN, MSNBC, and CBS News, and her writing has appeared in TIME, USA Today, Newsweek, Slate, Scientific American, The Hill, and many others. She was named to the San Francisco Business Times 40 Under 40. In film, she has supported projects that bring greater visibility and humanity to serious illness, death, and dying. She executive produced Netflix’s Oscar-nominated documentary End Game, supported the Oscar-nominated documentary Extremis, and executive produced Last Train Home and Robin’s Wish, a documentary about the final years of actor and comedian Robin Williams. She serves as secretary of the Board of Trustees of the Sutter Health CPMC Foundation and on the advisory boards of the Providence Institute for Human Caring and JScreen.

events.title: BOOK LAUNCH: Literature and Emergency Law in Kashmir and Northern Ireland
events.description:
The Department of African and African American Studies (DAAAS) in collaboration with the Center for South Asia (CSA) cordially invite the Stanford Community for a special book launch!

We are excited to celebrate the publication of a new book by our visiting postdoctoral scholar, Danny Shanhan titled, Literature and Emergency Law in Kashmir and Northern Ireland.

This book is the first substantial study of emergency law's relationship to literature in either the Northern Irish or the Kashmiri conflict and develops an original legal history that links these laws to a shared British colonial root. Engaging a wide range of fiction, poetry and film, from canonical poets Seamus Heaney and Agha Shahid Ali to contemporary works by Anna Burns, Mirza Waheed, and Bollywood filmmaker Vishal Bhardwaj, the book examines the literary response to the suspension of normative legal rights such as habeas corpus, the right to silence and even, in Kashmir, the right to life. By bringing these literary cultures together for the first time, it develops a literary and legal history that reveals common roots in colonial-era jurisprudence. The book re-situates these corpora, often isolated in scholarly work, as important parts of the global, material legacies of colonialism.

events.title: Eitner Lecture with M. D. Usher, "Journey to the West: Buddhists in Ancient Alexandria"
events.description:
Reception: Stanford Archaeology Center (500-106). Appetizers and drinks provided from 5:00 p.m. to 5:30 p.m.

Talk description: The recent discovery of a Buddha statue in Berenike---the first West of Afghanistan---confirms the presence of Buddhists in Hellenistic Egypt. This talk argues that the Therapeutae, a monastic community of men and women described by Philo of Alexandria in On the Contemplative Life---long thought to be Jewish---were actually Buddhist.

Short bio: M. D. Usher is the Lyman-Roberts Professor Classical Languages and Literature at the University of Vermont. He teaches and writes on topics related to the environment, agriculture, traditional crafts, sustainability, utopian thinking, ancient philosophy, and oral art forms. He has just completed a biography of Plotinus for Princeton.

The Lorenz Eitner Lectures on Classical Art and Culture publicize classics and classical scholarship to a wider public. The series has been endowed by Peter and Lindsay Joost, great friends and benefactors of Stanford Classics, in honor of the late Lorenz Eitner, director of Stanford’s art museum, now known as the Cantor Center, in the 1960s-80s. He also chaired what was then the Department of Art and Architecture and was a distinguished expert of French Romantic painting, and the author of a dozen books on art and art history. In naming these annual lectures after him, we honor the memory of a renowned scholar, teacher and writer who oversaw the expansion of our art museum to a leading regional art collection.

This event is also sponsored by the Stanford Archaeology Center.

This talk will not be available on zoom and will not be recorded.

events.title: November Museum Minis: Storytime at the Anderson
events.description:
Museum Minis is a welcoming monthly storytime at the Anderson Collection for children ages 0–5 and their caregivers. Each session features two engaging, age-appropriate books inspired by the essential elements of art—line, color, shape, and texture—introducing young children to these ideas and connecting them to artworks in the museum’s collection. Together, families are invited to look closely, notice details, and experience the museum environment in an accessible, joyful way. The Anderson Collection is home to works by artists such as Jackson Pollock, Mark Rothko, Joan Mitchell, and Nick Cave. The morning concludes with a light snack and time to connect.

Our storyteller, Maria, is a Visitor Experience Assistant and Museum Engagement Guide at the Anderson Collection. She brings a deep love of art, storytelling, and community to her work, and believes that every artwork — and every person — holds a story worth sharing. Outside the museum, she enjoys prioritizing wellness and slowing down with a good cup of tea.

No RSVP necessary, walk-ins welcome!

events.title: Galicia's Promised City with Oskar Czendze
events.description:
Between 1890 and 1914, tens of thousands of Jews from Galicia—the easternmost crownland of the Habsburg Empire—made New York City their new home. Yet their distinct experience has often been overshadowed by national narratives centered on migration from the Russian Empire. Oskar Czendze (University of Toronto) will explores how Galician Jews carried forms of regional and supranational belonging shaped in East Central Europe into New York.
